Assessment, omission and prediction targets

Source: vignettes/naboer.Rmd
naboer.Rmd

A fold assesses observations whose predictions contribute to a criterion and omits observations unavailable during fitting. Assessment is a subset of omission; the difference is an exclusion buffer. Analysis is the complement of omission.

x <- tibble::tibble(time = 1:8, y = c(1, 2, 2, 4, 3, 5, 7, 6))
folds <- custom_folds(x, assessment = list(3L, 6L), omission = list(2:4, 5:7))
tibble::as_tibble(folds, membership = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 8
#>   fold  n_assessment n_omission n_analysis n_buffer omitted_fraction assessment
#>   <chr>        <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>            <dbl> <list>    
#> 1 1                1          3          5        2            0.375 <int [1]> 
#> 2 2                1          3          5        2            0.375 <int [1]> 
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: omission <list>
as_nei(folds)
#> $a
#> [1] 2 3 4 5 6 7
#> 
#> $ma
#> [1] 3 6
#> 
#> $d
#> [1] 3 6
#> 
#> $md
#> [1] 1 2

nei$a concatenates omission indices; ma contains cumulative endpoints. d and md encode assessment. The first endpoint starts at position one; there is no leading zero. Repeated assessment across folds is retained, including its effect on the criterion. No automatic fold weighting is applied.

Prediction target Design
Beyond local residual dependence Focal neighbourhoods, optionally buffered blocks
New locations in the sampled region Spatial block holdouts
New periods Temporal blocks
Future observations Forecast origins, horizon and gap
New groups Whole-group or hierarchical holdouts
New environments Predictor-space clusters or strata
New taxa Phylogenetic clades, distance blocks or neighbourhoods

These designs pose different questions. Blocked validation can require extrapolation in predictors; a large error does not automatically imply a poor interpolation model. Choose dependence radii using scientific knowledge or separate diagnostics; naboer does not infer them automatically.

Model alignment and mgcv

Prepare complete modelling data first. Constructors preserve canonical order. fold_data() returns that order; as_nei(data = ...) can check it. With id, alignment checks compare identifiers; otherwise all canonical columns must match. Rebuild folds after changing observations.

all_folds <- loo_folds(x)
fit <- mgcv::gam(y ~ s(time, k = 4),
  data = fold_data(all_folds),
  method = "NCV", nei = as_nei(all_folds), na.action = stats::na.fail
)
fit$sp
#>  s(time) 
#> 28199.07

gam() supports NCV and QNCV; bam() supports NCV with discrete = TRUE. Leave jackknife unspecified to preserve mgcv’s covariance default. For sampled bam criteria, keep every neighbourhood and supply sample through as_nei(). Discarding unsampled definitions changes the information available for covariance.

A valid design does not guarantee approximation accuracy. Compare with exact refits for representative models, particularly for large omission fractions. benchmarks/approximation.R provides a reproducible fixed-basis study.

References

Roberts et al. (2017), Cross-validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure, Ecography 40:913–929. doi:10.1111/ecog.02881.

Wood, On Neighbourhood Cross Validation, arXiv:2404.16490.
